hero.title: Data Engineering Fundamentals
hero.subtitle: Learn the ideas behind every data platform, and practise the SQL: dimensional modelling, slowly changing history, deduplication, incremental loads and data-quality tests.

faq.q: Does the code run in the browser?
faq.a: The SQL does: the practice window runs a SQL engine on built-in raw tables, and nothing leaves your device. Python, Spark, Airflow and Kafka are shown as annotated code to read or to run in your own environment; the lessons say where.

faq.q: Which cloud or tool does it teach?
faq.a: None in particular. It teaches the ideas that hold across warehouses, lakes, orchestrators and streaming systems, and names tools as examples. Check each vendor's current documentation when you choose one.
SQL basics. SQL for Data & Business in this category is the best preparation; Data Analytics with Python & SQL helps too.

Running a cluster, an orchestrator or a streaming platform. They need infrastructure, so they are taught with scenarios, listings and sorting activities, while the modelling, transformation and testing, which are the core of the job, run here.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your Yugty profile. It is not a vendor certification.

activities.title: Build the type 2 customer history
activities.objective: Build validity dates from a change log with LEAD.
activities.scenario: customer_changes records every city a customer has lived in and when they moved in. Build the type 2 history: `customer_id`, `city`, `valid_from` (the change date), `valid_to` (the date of the next change, or '9999-12-31' for the current city) and `is_current` (1 for the current city, otherwise 0). Sort by customer_id, then valid_from.
steps: Use LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) to find the next change.
is_current is 1 where there is no next change.

checks.label: Your query runs without an error
checks.hint: Press Run query and read any message under the editor: it names the problem.
checks.explain: A query that does not run cannot be checked. The message tells you which word or column it could not understand.

checks.label: It uses LEAD
checks.hint: The task needs LEAD. Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: LEAD is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It uses a window function
checks.hint: The task needs a window function. Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: A window function is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It returns the right rows and columns
checks.hint: Compare the number of rows and columns you get with what the task describes, then check your conditions.
checks.explain: LEAD reads the next change for the same customer; that date is when this version stops. The last version has no next change, so it gets the far-future date and is current.

spec.solution: SELECT customer_id, city, changed_at AS valid_from, COALESCE(LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at), '9999-12-31') AS valid_to, CASE WHEN LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_current FROM customer_changes ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from

checks.label: The rows are in the order the task asks for
checks.hint: Check the ORDER BY: which column, and ascending or descending?
checks.explain: The task names the sort order; a second sort column breaks ties.

spec.solution: SELECT customer_id, city, changed_at AS valid_from, COALESCE(LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at), '9999-12-31') AS valid_to, CASE WHEN LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS is_current FROM customer_changes ORDER BY customer_id, valid_from

activities.title: Which city was it then?
activities.objective: Join facts to the dimension version that was valid at the time.
activities.scenario: For every order show `order_id`, `order_date` and `city`: the city the customer lived in **on the order date**. Build the type 2 versions in a CTE (as in the previous lab, without is_current) and join with a half-open date range. Every order must match exactly one version. Sort by order_id.
steps: WITH v AS (...) builds customer_id, city, valid_from, valid_to.
Join orders to v on customer_id and order_date >= valid_from AND order_date < valid_to.

spec.solution: WITH v AS (SELECT customer_id, city, changed_at AS valid_from, COALESCE(LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at), '9999-12-31') AS valid_to FROM customer_changes) SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, v.city FROM orders o JOIN v ON v.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_date >= v.valid_from AND o.order_date < v.valid_to ORDER BY o.order_id

activities.title: Latest status per order
activities.objective: Remove duplicate deliveries, then keep the newest event for each order.
activities.scenario: order_events is a raw log: some events were delivered twice, and events for an order can arrive out of order. Return `order_id` and `status` of the **latest** event for every order (by event_ts; break ties with the larger event_id), after removing the duplicate deliveries. Sort by order_id.
steps: First SELECT DISTINCT the event columns.
Number the rows per order, newest first, with ROW_NUMBER.

activities.scenario: Finance counts an order as revenue only when its **latest** status is 'delivered'. Build the mart: `month` (the first seven characters of the order_date from the orders table), `delivered_orders` (how many) and `revenue` (the sum of amount from the latest event). Sort by month.

activities.title: Quality checks on the payments feed
activities.objective: Write several data-quality tests as one query.
activities.scenario: The payments feed arrives from another system. Return one row counting each kind of problem: `null_orders` (payments with no order_id), `duplicate_payments` (rows beyond the distinct payment_id values), `negative_amounts` (amount below zero), `orphan_payments` (an order_id that does not exist in orders) and `bad_methods` (method not one of 'card', 'upi', 'cod').
steps: Use COUNT(*) - COUNT(col) for nulls and COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT payment_id) for duplicates.
SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) counts a condition.
For orphans: order_id IS NOT NULL AND order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders).

checks.label: Your query runs without an error
checks.hint: Press Run query and read any message under the editor: it names the problem.
checks.explain: A query that does not run cannot be checked. The message tells you which word or column it could not understand.

checks.label: It uses CASE
checks.hint: The task needs CASE. Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: CASE is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It returns the right rows and columns
checks.hint: Compare the number of rows and columns you get with what the task describes, then check your conditions.
checks.explain: Each column is one test that counts violations: nulls (COUNT difference), duplicates (COUNT DISTINCT difference), a range test, a relationships test and an accepted-values test. A healthy feed would return zeros.

spec.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(order_id) AS null_orders, COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT payment_id) AS duplicate_payments, SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS negative_amounts, SUM(CASE WHEN order_id IS NOT NULL AND order_id NOT IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS orphan_payments, SUM(CASE WHEN method NOT IN ('card', 'upi', 'cod') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS bad_methods FROM payments

activities.title: Orders created per two-hour window
activities.objective: Aggregate events into tumbling time windows.
activities.scenario: Group the **created** events into two-hour windows by the hour of event_ts (8, 10, 12, ...). Return `hour_window` (the start hour of the window, as a number such as 8, 10 or 12) and `orders` (how many different orders had a created event in that window). Sort by hour_window.
steps: The hour is CAST(SUBSTR(event_ts, 12, 2) AS INTEGER).
Filter status = 'created', COUNT DISTINCT order_id, GROUP BY 1.

activities.title: Revenue by customer city, as it was then
activities.objective: Combine deduplication, the latest event, a business rule and a type 2 join in one pipeline query.
activities.scenario: Finance wants delivered revenue by the city each customer lived in **when they ordered**. Return `city`, `orders` (how many delivered orders) and `revenue` (the sum of the amount from each order's latest event). An order counts only if its latest status (after removing duplicate deliveries) is 'delivered'. Sort by revenue descending, then city.
steps: CTE 1: the deduplicated events with ROW_NUMBER per order (newest first).
CTE 2: the type 2 customer versions with LEAD.
Join the latest delivered events to orders, then to the version valid on the order date, and aggregate by city.

checks.label: Your query runs without an error
checks.hint: Press Run query and read any message under the editor: it names the problem.
checks.explain: A query that does not run cannot be checked. The message tells you which word or column it could not understand.

checks.label: It uses CTEs (WITH)
checks.hint: The task needs CTEs (WITH). Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: CTEs (WITH) is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It uses ROW_NUMBER for the latest event
checks.hint: The task needs ROW_NUMBER for the latest event. Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: ROW_NUMBER for the latest event is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It uses LEAD for the customer versions
checks.hint: The task needs LEAD for the customer versions. Think about which clause does that job.
checks.explain: LEAD for the customer versions is the tool built for this part of the task.

checks.label: It returns the right rows and columns
checks.hint: Compare the number of rows and columns you get with what the task describes, then check your conditions.
checks.explain: Dedupe and keep the latest event per order, build the type 2 versions with LEAD, join the order date into the version's half-open range, and aggregate. Every order matches one event and one customer version, so no total is inflated.

spec.solution: WITH l AS (SELECT order_id, status, amount, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC) AS rn FROM (SELECT DISTINCT event_id, order_id, status, amount, event_ts FROM order_events) d), v AS (SELECT customer_id, city, changed_at AS valid_from, COALESCE(LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at), '9999-12-31') AS valid_to FROM customer_changes) SELECT v.city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(l.amount) AS revenue FROM l JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = l.order_id JOIN v ON v.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o.order_date >= v.valid_from AND o.order_date < v.valid_to WHERE l.rn = 1 AND l.status = 'delivered' GROUP BY v.city ORDER BY revenue DESC, v.city

checks.label: The rows are in the order the task asks for
